locators: p. 93, Line 12, "Certain business expenses of National Guard and reserve members who traveled more than 100 miles from home"
p. 93, Line 14, "You can deduct moving expenses if you are a member of the Armed Forces on active duty and due to a military order you move because of a permanent change of station"
p. 95, Line 20, "Don’t include any repayments of qualified reservist distributions"

findings.who: A county constable, justice of the peace or coroner who is paid fees for the office and receives no Form W-2. The fees may be collected directly from the public or reported on a Form 1099. The filer (or spouse) has no Form W-2 on the return.
findings.why_no: The computed gate is false whenever no Form W-2 is listed, so the artist/official question is never asked. Fee-basis pay often comes with no W-2.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 93, Line 12: 'Include the following deductions on line 12. ... • Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials.'
findings.fix: Do not condition the official branch on a Form W-2. Ask the official part of scope.artist_official on every return. Keep the W-2 condition, if at all, only for the performing-artist branch.

findings.who: A performer who worked as an employee for two or more theater or orchestra employers, but one or both employers wrongly issued a Form 1099 or no form. The filer reports those wages on Form 8919 (or on a Form 4852 substitute) and lists no Form W-2.
findings.why_no: The gate is computed false because no Form W-2 is listed. Yet the filer was an employee performing artist, and the line depends on that fact, not on the form.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 93, Line 12: '• Performing-arts-related expenses as a qualified performing artist.' ... 'For more details, see Form 2106.'
findings.fix: Widen the gate to 'a Form W-2 is listed, or wages are reported on Form 8919 or a substitute W-2 (Form 4852)'. Or ask the artist question whenever there are any wages on line 1a or 1g.

findings.who: An office worker (or the spouse) who also took paid gigs as an employee musician, actor or dancer for two small employers during 2025, with low AGI.
findings.why_no: 'Did you work as a performing artist' reads as a question about occupation. Someone whose main job is something else answers no, though performing-arts services as an employee for two employers can qualify.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 93, Line 12: 'Performing-arts-related expenses as a qualified performing artist.'
findings.fix: Reword: 'In 2025, were you (or your spouse) paid as an employee for any performing-arts work (acting, music, dance, etc.), even as a side job or for only part of the year?'

findings.who: A state or local government employee (not elected or appointed to an office) who is paid a salary plus fees, for example a deputy clerk or registrar who keeps part of the filing fees.
findings.why_no: 'Official' suggests an officeholder. 'Paid from fees' suggests pay made up entirely of fees. A salaried employee who gets fees only in part answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi 2025 p. 93, Line 12: '• Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials.' (see Form 2106)
findings.fix: Reword: 'In 2025, were you (or your spouse) employed by a state or local government and paid in whole or in part by fees?'

locators: p. 93, Line 12, "Performing-arts-related expenses as a qualified performing artist", "Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials"

p. 93, Line 12, "Performing-arts-related expenses as a qualified performing artist", "Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials"; p. 93, Line 12, "For more details, see Form 2106"

findings.who: A filer, or their spouse on a joint return, who first bought a limited-partnership or LLC interest, or a stake in a business they do not help run, during 2025. The activity produced a loss or income in 2025, or the interest was bought and sold within 2025.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about 'any year before 2025'. Someone whose first ownership began in 2025 truthfully answers no, so the passive-activity question, and the refusal it leads to, is never reached.
findings.irs_text: i8582 p. 1: "Form 8582 is filed by individuals, estates, and trusts who have passive activity deductions" and "passive activities include … Trade or business activities in which you did not materially participate for the tax year."
findings.fix: Ask the passive question regardless of the before-2025 gate. Alternatively, widen the gate to 'In 2025 or any earlier year, did you (or your spouse) own or have an interest in …'.

findings.who: A filer who holds units of a publicly traded partnership (MLP) in a brokerage account, or who is a member of a multi-member LLC taxed as a partnership. They receive a Schedule K-1 (Form 1065).
findings.why_no: They read 'a share of a partnership' as a law-firm-style partnership. They think of their holding as stock-like 'units' or as an 'LLC', not a partnership, so they answer no. The Form 8986 question and the passive question are then skipped.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 34, Line 16: "Tax from Form 8978, line 14 (relating to partner’s audit liability under section 6226)"; i8582 p. 1: "passive activities include … Trade or business activities in which you did not materially participate."
findings.fix: Ask 'Did you or your spouse ever receive a Schedule K-1 (Form 1065 or 1120-S), or own an interest in an LLC, a publicly traded partnership (MLP units), a partnership or an S corporation?'

findings.who: A beneficiary of a trust or estate that holds a partnership interest or runs a business. The beneficiary receives a Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) carrying passive income, or a pushed-out Form 8986 through the trust or estate as a pass-through partner.
findings.why_no: A beneficiary does not 'own' a business or 'a share of a partnership', so they truthfully answer the gate no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 34, Line 16: "Tax from Form 8978, line 14 (relating to partner’s audit liability under section 6226)"; i8582 p. 1: "Form 8582 is filed by individuals, estates, and trusts who have passive activity deductions."
findings.fix: Add to the gate: 'or were you a beneficiary of a trust or estate that sent you a Schedule K-1 (Form 1041) or a Form 8986?'

findings.who: A former freelancer, independent contractor, gig worker or rideshare driver who filed Schedule C before 2025. They elected section 179 on equipment such as a vehicle, computer or camera, and part of the deduction was disallowed by the business income limit.
findings.why_no: They do not think of side work as 'owning a business', so they answer the gate no. The section 179 carryover question is never asked.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 5, Line 10: "The carryover of disallowed deduction from 2024 is the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed as a deduction because of the business income limitation."
findings.fix: Reword the gate as 'own or run a business (including self-employment, freelance or gig work reported on Schedule C or F) …'. Alternatively, gate the carryover on 'Did you file Form 4562 for 2024 or any earlier year?'

findings.who: A filer whose before-2025 business interest was held through a single-member LLC or another entity whose name does not match the listed words. Section 179 or passive items flowed to them through that entity.
findings.why_no: They read 'a business, a farm, a rental property, or a share of a partnership or an S corporation' as a complete list of entity types. They think 'I had an LLC', which is none of these, and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i4562 p. 5, Line 6(c): "To report your share of a section 179 expense deduction from a partnership or an S corporation, enter 'from Schedule K-1 (Form 1065)' or 'from Schedule K-1 (Form 1120-S)'."
findings.fix: Add help text: 'Count an interest held through an LLC, whether single- or multi-member, and any interest for which you received a Schedule K-1.'

locators: p. 5, Line 10, "The carryover of disallowed deduction from 2024 is the amount of section 179 property, if any, you elected to expense in previous years that was not allowed as a deduction because of the business income limitation" and "If you filed Form 4562 for 2024, enter the amount from line 13 of your 2024 Form 4562" (owner: the printed amount)
, Purpose of Form, "Form 8582 is used by noncorporate taxpayers to figure the amount of any passive activity loss (PAL)"
p. 34, Line 16, "Tax from Form 8978, line 14 (relating to partner’s audit liability under section 6226)"

used.how: pages named by another document's citation

findings.who: A filer is a partner in a U.S. hedge fund or other domestic flow-through fund that owns shares of a foreign PFIC and sells them in 2025; the fund itself is a U.S. fund, but the filer may be an indirect PFIC shareholder.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'not through a U.S. fund,' so they answer no; the help's 'partnership' line does not say U.S. or foreign, and they read the U.S.-fund exclusion as covering their domestic fund.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 34, Line 16: 'Any tax from Form 8621, line 16e, relating to a section 1291 fund'; p. 114, Line 17p: 'Enter any interest amount from Form 8621, line 16f, relating to distributions from, and dispositions of, stock of a section 1291 fund.'
findings.fix: Narrow the exclusion to a U.S. mutual fund/ETF/RIC that reports the foreign shares to the filer, and state that foreign shares held through a U.S. partnership, LLC, or grantor trust still count.

findings.who: A filer owns all or part of a foreign LLC or other foreign company through membership units, percentage interests, or similar equity, and the entity is taxed as a corporation, so it can be a CFC or PFIC.
findings.why_no: The gate asks about 'shares or options'; the filer holds membership units or equity interests, not shares or options, so answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 91, Line 8n: 'Section 951 generally requires that a U.S. shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation include in income its pro rata share'; p. 34, Line 16: 'Any tax from Form 8621, line 16e, relating to a section 1291 fund.'
findings.fix: Ask about 'shares, membership interests, units, or other equity, or options' and explain that foreign LLC/company interests taxed as corporate stock count.

findings.who: A filer sold a foreign fund in March 2025 and no longer holds it at year-end or when filing.
findings.why_no: They read 'In 2025, did you hold' as asking about shares held at the end of 2025 or at filing, so answer no; the March sale itself is a 2025 disposition.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 114, Line 17p: 'Enter any interest amount from Form 8621, line 16f, relating to distributions from, and dispositions of, stock of a section 1291 fund.'
findings.fix: Say 'at any time during 2025, including shares you sold, exchanged, or otherwise disposed of in 2025.'

locators: p. 34, Line 16, "Any tax from Form 8621, line 16e, relating to a section 1291 fund"; p. 114, Line 17p, "Enter any interest amount from Form 8621, line 16f"

p. 91, Line 8n, "Section 951 generally requires that a U.S. shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation include in income its pro rata share"; p. 91, Line 8o, "Section 951A generally requires that a U.S. shareholder of a controlled foreign corporation include in income its global intangible low-taxed income"

findings.who: A joint filer (or spouse) with a W-2 that reports in box 1 a pension or annuity from a nonqualified deferred compensation plan, while box 11 is blank.
findings.why_no: The question asks only whether box 11 shows the payment. The filer checks box 11, sees it blank, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1a: If you received a pension or annuity from a nonqualified deferred compensation plan or a nongovernmental section 457 plan and it was reported in box 1 of Form W-2, do not include this amount on Form 1040, line 1a. This amount is reported on Schedule 1, line 8t.
findings.fix: Ask about the fact of such a pension or annuity and whether it was shown on a W-2, whether in box 1 or box 11, or on Form 1099-R; do not ask only about box 11.

findings.who: A filer (or spouse) who receives a nongovernmental section 457 plan distribution reported on Form 1099-R and has no W-2.
findings.why_no: The W-2 gate is false, so the question is not asked; a W-2-only box 11 question would also be answered no.
findings.irs_text: f1040s1 p. 1, line 8t: Pension or annuity from a nonqualified deferred compensation plan or a nongovernmental section 457 plan.
findings.fix: Remove the W-2-only gate and ask about these pensions and annuities regardless of whether reported on a W-2 or Form 1099-R.

findings.who: An employee (or spouse) with a W-2 whose box 8 is blank and whose box 12 has none of codes A, B, K, M, N, or Z, but who received $20 or more of cash tips in a month and did not report the full amount to the employer.
findings.why_no: The question lists only box 8 and those codes, so the filer truthfully answers no; the W-2 does not show the uncollected tax on the unreported tips.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 112, Line 5: If you received tips of $20 or more in any month and you didn't report the full amount to your employer, you must pay the social security and Medicare tax on the unreported tips.
findings.fix: Add a question about unreported tips of $20 or more in any month, or broaden this scope question to include that fact.

findings.who: A filer (or spouse) whose nonqualified deferred compensation plan failed section 409A and the income is reported in box 15 of Form 1099-MISC, with no W-2 code Z, including a return with no W-2.
findings.why_no: The question asks only whether a W-2 has code Z; the W-2 does not, or there is no W-2, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 114, Line 17h: This income should be shown in box 12 of Form W-2 with code Z, or in box 15 of Form 1099-MISC.
findings.fix: Ask about a section 409A failure and 1099-MISC box 15 as well as W-2 code Z; do not make the W-2 gate exclusive.

findings.who: A filer (or spouse) who received an excess parachute payment reportable in box 3 of Form 1099-NEC and has no W-2 code K, including a return with no W-2.
findings.why_no: The question asks only whether a W-2 shows code K; it does not, so the filer answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 114, Line 17k: If you received a Form 1099-NEC, the tax is 20% of the EPP shown in box 3.
findings.fix: Ask about excess parachute payments on Form 1099-NEC box 3 as well as W-2 code K.

findings.who: A state or local government official (or spouse) compensated solely on a fee basis, with no W-2, who paid business expenses deductible on Schedule 1 line 12.
findings.why_no: The W-2 gate is false, so the question is not asked; if asked, the filer would answer yes to being paid from fees.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 93, Line 12: Performing-arts-related expenses as a qualified performing artist; Business expenses of fee-basis state or local government officials.
findings.fix: Remove the W-2-only gate or ask the question regardless of W-2; a fee-basis official may have no W-2.

findings.who: A filer (or spouse) under 50 with only SIMPLE plan(s) who deferred $18,000 for 2025.
findings.why_no: The question states the yearly limit is $23,500 for most people, and $18,000 is not more than $23,500, so they answer no; the SIMPLE limit is $16,500.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1h: This limit is generally (a) $16,500 if you have only SIMPLE plans, and (b) $26,500 for section 403(b) plans if you qualify for the 15-year rule in Pub. 571.
findings.fix: Ask about the applicable plan-specific limit and state the SIMPLE, 403(b) 15-year, catch-up, and 457(b) rules in the help.

findings.who: A filer (or spouse) with two separate 457(b) plans at two jobs who deferred $12,000 to each, $24,000 total, and read 'count it apart' as applying separately to each 457(b) plan.
findings.why_no: They compare each $12,000 plan to the limit and answer no, though the 457(b) limit is an aggregate per-person limit under all such plans.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1h: If the total amount you (or your spouse if filing jointly) deferred for 2025 under all plans was more than $23,500, include the excess on line 1h.
findings.fix: Say that multiple 457(b) plans are aggregated for the same person and that 'apart' means apart from 401(k) or 403(b), not apart plan-by-plan.

findings.who: A full-time life insurance salesperson (or spouse) who is a statutory employee but whose employer did not check the Statutory employee box in box 13.
findings.why_no: The question asks whether the box is ticked. It is not, so the filer answers no even though the filer was a statutory employee by occupation.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 25, Were You a Statutory Employee?: If you were a statutory employee, the Statutory employee box in box 13 of your Form W-2 should be checked. Statutory employees include full-time life insurance salespeople.
findings.fix: Ask about the statutory-employee categories and facts, not only whether the employer checked box 13.

findings.who: A filer (or spouse) who contributed through payroll to a section 501(c)(18)(D) pension plan but whose W-2 box 12 does not show code H.
findings.why_no: The question asks only whether box 12 shows code H; with no code H the filer answers no, although the contribution is deductible on Schedule 1 line 24f.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 100, Line 24f: Enter contributions to section 501(c)(18) (D) pension plans (see Pub. 525).
findings.fix: Ask about section 501(c)(18)(D) contributions directly and accept plan records, not only W-2 code H.

findings.who: A statutory employee, for example a full-time life insurance salesperson, who received no W-2 and therefore has no box 13 mark or code H.
findings.why_no: The W-2 gate is false, so the statutory-employee question is never asked and the tool treats the line as no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 25: Statutory employees report the amount shown in box 1 of Form W-2 on a Schedule C. Even if you don't get a Form W-2, you must still report your earnings.
findings.fix: Ask about statutory-employee status by occupation and facts even when no W-2 was received, and handle missing W-2 earnings.

findings.who: A household employee such as a nanny or housekeeper whose household issued a Form W-2 for part of the 2025 pay but paid an additional cash amount that the W-2 did not report.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether the household 'gave you no W-2'; this household did give a W-2, so the literal and truthful answer is no, even though some household-employee wages were omitted from it.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: "Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2."
findings.fix: Gate on whether any household-employee wages were not reported on a W-2, even if the household issued a W-2 for other wages; change 'gave you no W-2' to 'did not report all of your household wages on a W-2.'

findings.who: A nanny, housekeeper, or caregiver paid directly by a family that gave no W-2 but issued a Form 1099-NEC or told the filer they were an independent contractor.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether they were paid 'as a household employee.' The filer may read the 1099 or contractor label as meaning they were not an employee and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: "Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2."
findings.fix: Ask the observable facts (work in or around a home for its members, paid by the household, no W-2) and state that a 1099 or contractor label does not by itself make the worker a non-employee.

findings.who: A filer paid less than $2,800 in 2025 by a household for nanny, housekeeping, or similar work and given no W-2.
findings.why_no: The gate asks about 'wages ... not on a W-2,' but the filer may think pay below the W-2 threshold is not 'wages' or is not reportable because no W-2 was required; the $2,800 help appears only after the gate.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: "Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2. An employer isn’t required to provide a Form W-2 to you if they paid you wages of less than $2,800 in 2025."
findings.fix: Put the $2,800 point in the gate or ask 'Did any household pay you wages not reported on a W-2, even if the amount was under $2,800?'

findings.who: A filer who worked for the same household in 2024, received a W-2 for that year, and worked again in 2025 for cash with no 2025 W-2.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether the household 'gave you no W-2' without saying for 2025; the filer may remember the 2024 W-2 and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: "Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2."
findings.fix: Specify 'no W-2 for that 2025 pay' or '2025 household wages not reported on a 2025 W-2.'

locators: p. 24, Line 1b, "Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2"

p. 24, Line 1b, "Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2", "An employer isn’t required to provide a Form W-2 to you if they paid you wages of less than $2,800 in 2025"

findings.who: A caregiver paid through a state Medicaid waiver, agency, or care plan to care for a disabled client in the client's home rather than the caregiver's own home, who receives a Form 1099-MISC/NEC or no W-2 and is not in a separate home-care trade or business.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether the person cared for was 'living in your home'; the help says caring for someone who does not live with you is paid work in someone's home. This filer truthfully answers no because the care recipient does not live in the filer's home.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1d: 'Enter your taxable Medicaid waiver payments that were not reported on Form(s) W-2' and 'enter on Form 1040, line 1d, your Medicaid waiver payments reported on Form 1099-MISC or Form 1099-NEC.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to ask whether the filer or spouse received any Medicaid waiver/difficulty-of-care payments, including taxable payments for caring for someone outside the filer's home; or add a separate taxable-Medicaid-waiver question that feeds Form 1040 line 1d.

findings.who: A filer paid under a Medicaid waiver to care for someone living in the filer's home, but paid by Form 1099-MISC/NEC or with no form, so the filer has no W-2 with code II and wants to include the nontaxable payments in earned income for a credit.
findings.why_no: The help says 'A W-2 with code II in box 12 shows them'; the filer reads that as the only way such payments are identified and answers no when no W-2/code II exists.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1d: payments 'not reported on Form(s) W-2, or not reported in box 1 of Form(s) W-2'; and p. 92, Line 8s: 'If you did not receive a Form W-2 for nontaxable payments ... report the amount on Form 1040 ... line 1d.'
findings.fix: State that a W-2 code II is only one way these payments appear; ask about Medicaid waiver/difficulty-of-care payments even if reported on Form 1099-MISC/NEC or no form.

findings.who: A filer who in 2025 receives a final Medicaid waiver payment for care provided in 2024 while the care recipient lived with them, but the recipient moved out or died before the 2025 payment.
findings.why_no: The gate says 'In 2025 ... to care for someone living in your home'; the filer reads 'living' as requiring the person to live there when paid in 2025, so answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 92, Line 8s: 'Certain Medicaid waiver payments you received for caring for someone living in your home with you may be nontaxable'; 'If nontaxable payments were reported to you in box 1 of Form(s) W-2, report the amount on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1a.'
findings.fix: Ask whether the 2025 payment was for care of someone who lived with the filer when the care was provided, even if the person no longer lives there; avoid present-tense 'living.'

locators: p. 24, Line 1d, "Also enter the total of your taxable and nontaxable Medicaid waiver payments that were not reported on Form(s) W-2, or not reported in box 1 of Form(s) W-2"

p. 24, Line 1d, "Also enter the total of your taxable and nontaxable Medicaid waiver payments that were not reported on Form(s) W-2, or not reported in box 1 of Form(s) W-2"; p. 92, Line 8s, "Your nontaxable Medicaid waiver payments should be reported to you on Form(s) W-2 in box 12, Code II"

p. 92, Line 8s, "Nontaxable amount of Medicaid waiver payments included on Form 1040, line 1a or 1d", "If nontaxable payments were reported to you in box 1 of Form(s) W-2, report the amount on Form 1040 or 1040-SR, line 1a"

findings.who: A filer whose only carried-forward NOL arose from pre-2018 employee business expenses or moving expenses.
findings.why_no: The help lists only business, farm, rental, disaster, or Form 461 losses; employee work and moving expenses are omitted, so the filer reads the loss as outside the gate.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 1: 'To have an NOL, your loss must generally be caused by deductions from your: ... Work as an employee ... Moving expenses ...'
findings.fix: Add employee business expenses and moving expenses to the help, or ask broadly whether any Form 172 or prior-year NOL carryforward is being carried into 2025.

findings.who: A qualified performing artist, Armed Forces reservist, fee-basis state or local official, or active-duty service member with a post-2017 NOL from employee business expenses or moving expenses.
findings.why_no: The same omitted categories apply; the filer has an NOL from work as an employee or moving expenses, not from the listed business, farm, rental, disaster, or Form 461 sources.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 1: 'Work as an employee (although not deductible for most taxpayers for 2018 through 2025)' and 'Moving expenses (although not deductible for most taxpayers for 2018 through 2025)' are NOL causes, so exceptions remain.
findings.fix: Broaden the help to include employee business expenses and moving expenses, including current-year exceptions, or ask whether prior-year Form 172 shows an NOL carryforward.

findings.who: A filer with an NOL from a year in which total business or rental deductions exceeded income, but no single business, farm, rental, or disaster loss was larger than that year's income.
findings.why_no: The help says 'A loss bigger than that year's income,' which can be read as requiring one loss to exceed income; the NOL instead comes from combined deductions.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 1: 'If your deductions for the year are more than your income for the year, you may have a net operating loss.'
findings.fix: Say that deductions for the loss year exceeded income, rather than 'a loss bigger than that year's income.'

findings.who: A filer whose original NOL was larger than the loss year's income but who has already used part of it, so the remaining unused carryforward is now smaller than that year's income.
findings.why_no: The help says 'A loss bigger than that year's income, not yet used up'; the filer reads the remaining unused amount as needing to be bigger than the loss year's income.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 2: 'If you carried the NOL to an earlier year, your NOL deduction is the carried over NOL minus the NOL amount you used in the earlier year or years.'
findings.fix: Clarify that the original loss must have exceeded the loss-year income and that a partially used remaining carryforward still qualifies.

findings.who: A filer with a prior-year passive rental loss that was suspended on Form 8582 but became allowed in an earlier year and generated an NOL carryforward into 2025.
findings.why_no: The help says 'Not a loss still held back on Form 8582'; seeing Form 8582 in the records, the filer reads any passive loss as excluded even though it is no longer held back.
findings.irs_text: i172 p. 1: 'To have an NOL, your loss must generally be caused by deductions from your: ... Rental property.'
findings.fix: Clarify that only losses still suspended under Form 8582 in 2025 are excluded; a previously suspended loss that became allowed and created an NOL is included.

locators: p. 91, Line 8a, "Enter any deduction for an NOL from an earlier year"

findings.who: A U.S. citizen who renounced citizenship in 2025, for example at a consulate in October, and lived abroad as a nonresident alien for the rest of the year. Alternatively, a joint filer whose spouse did this.
findings.why_no: The words "not a U.S. citizen" read like a question for immigrants. A former citizen who held citizenship for most of 2025, or who thinks of themselves as an American, may answer no. Nothing in the gate or its help mentions losing or renouncing citizenship during the year.
findings.line: scope.nonresident_if_noncitizen (gated scope.nonresident; a Yes would end the interview). After the no, the tool prepares a full-year Form 1040 for a dual-status filer.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 8: "Most nonresident aliens and dual-status aliens have different filing requirements and may have to file Form 1040-NR."
findings.fix: Ask: "At any time in 2025, were you (or your spouse, on a joint return) not a U.S. citizen? Answer Yes if either of you became a citizen, gave up or lost citizenship, or was never a citizen at any point in 2025." Alternatively, add a separate question: "Did you or your spouse renounce or lose U.S. citizenship, or give up a green card, in 2025?"

findings.who: A filer, or a spouse on a joint return, who naturalized in 2025 without a prior green card, for example through military-service naturalization, and was a nonresident alien before naturalizing.
findings.why_no: The filer is a citizen when filing. They may read the question as present-tense status ("are you a citizen?") and answer no, even though the question says "at any time in 2025".
findings.line: scope.nonresident_if_noncitizen (gated scope.nonresident). The filer was dual-status, but the tool continues as if they were a citizen all year.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 8: "Specific rules apply to determine if you are a resident alien, nonresident alien, or dual-status alien. Most nonresident aliens and dual-status aliens have different filing requirements and may have to file Form 1040-NR."
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Answer Yes if either of you became a U.S. citizen during 2025, even if you are a citizen now."

findings.who: A fiscal-year individual filer whose tax year begins in 2025 and ends in 2026, and who (or whose spouse) gave up citizenship or became a nonresident alien in the 2026 part of that tax year.
findings.why_no: The gate asks only about "any time in 2025", calendar year. The change happened in 2026, so the truthful answer is no.
findings.irs_text: f1040 (2025) p. 1 header: "For the year Jan. 1–Dec. 31, 2025, or other tax year beginning , 2025, ending , 20"; i1040gi p. 8 on Form 1040-NR for dual-status aliens.
findings.fix: Ask "at any time during your 2025 tax year". Alternatively, state that the tool handles only calendar-year filers.

locators: p. 8, "Most nonresident aliens and dual-status aliens have different filing requirements and may have to file Form 1040-NR"

findings.who: A filer whose employer issued a W-2 but the form was lost or never reached them, so the filer has pay stubs but no W-2 to enter.
findings.why_no: The gate asks for wages 'not on a W-2'; the filer reads that as wages not reported on the W-2 that exists, so answers no even though they have no W-2 in hand.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 25, Missing or Incorrect Form W-2?: If you lose your Form W-2 ... ask your employer for a new one. Even if you don’t get a Form W-2, you must still report your earnings.
findings.fix: Ask whether the filer has wages for which they did not receive a W-2, and treat a W-2 that is missing, lost, or never received as a Yes that triggers the ask-employer-first refusal.

findings.who: A filer whose employer has not sent a W-2 by filing time, or who never received it and expects it to arrive.
findings.why_no: The filer reads 'not on a W-2' as off-the-books pay or as not reportable until the W-2 arrives, so answers no rather than reporting earnings from pay stubs.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 25: Even if you don’t get a Form W-2, you must still report your earnings.
findings.fix: Include missing or not-yet-received W-2s in the gate help and ask whether the filer has wages for which no W-2 has been received.

findings.who: A filer received a W-2 that omits a bonus or part of the pay, so part of the wages is not on the W-2.
findings.why_no: Because a W-2 arrived, the filer reads the gate as asking whether they got a W-2 at all and answers no, missing the omitted wages.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 25: If you lose your Form W-2 or it is incorrect, ask your employer for a new one. Even if you don’t get a Form W-2, you must still report your earnings.
findings.fix: Mention incorrect or incomplete W-2s in the gate/help and ask whether any wages are missing from the W-2.

findings.who: A gardener, private driver, or live-in carer paid by a household for work around the home, for household members, or in a home the worker shares.
findings.why_no: The gate help says 'pay for work in someone's home'; the filer reads 'in' narrowly and does not count work around the home, for its members, or in a shared home.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2.
findings.fix: Use the broader gated wording in the gate help: work in or around a household's home or for its members, including a home the filer shares.

findings.who: A babysitter, cleaner, or other household worker paid less than $2,800 in cash by a household, with no W-2.
findings.why_no: The filer knows no W-2 is required below $2,800 and reads 'not on a W-2' as not reportable, so answers no.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1b: Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2. An employer isn’t required to provide a Form W-2 to you if they paid you wages of less than $2,800 in 2025.
findings.fix: Add to the gate help that household wages are reportable even when the household was not required to give a W-2 because it paid less than $2,800.

findings.who: A worker who performed services for a firm that treated the worker as a contractor but was paid through an agency, platform, or other intermediary rather than directly by the firm.
findings.why_no: The gate help says 'pay from a firm'; the worker reads that as requiring direct payment by the firm and answers no because the intermediary paid them.
findings.irs_text: f8919 p. 2, Firm: This firm may or may not have paid you directly for these services.
findings.fix: Ask whether the filer performed services for a firm that treated them as a contractor, even if payment came through someone else.

findings.who: A worker who received both a W-2 and a Form 1099-MISC or 1099-NEC from the same firm for 2025, where the 1099 amount should have been wages on the W-2.
findings.why_no: Because a W-2 came from the firm, the worker reads the gate as satisfied and answers no, even though the 1099 amount is not on any W-2.
findings.irs_text: f8919 p. 1, Reason code H: I received a Form W-2 and a Form 1099-MISC and/or 1099-NEC from this firm for 2025. The amount on Form 1099-MISC and/or 1099-NEC should have been included as wages on Form W-2.
findings.fix: Add a gate help example for a firm that gave both a W-2 and a 1099 for pay that should have been wages.

findings.who: A worker who believes they were an employee, filed Form SS-8, and has not received an IRS determination, while the firm paid them as a contractor with no social security or Medicare withholding.
findings.why_no: The gate help says 'wrongly treated you as a contractor'; the worker reads 'wrongly' as requiring an IRS determination and answers no because no reply has come.
findings.irs_text: f8919 p. 1: You believe your pay from the firm wasn’t for services as an independent contractor; reason code G: I filed Form SS-8 with the IRS and haven’t received a reply.
findings.fix: Ask whether the worker believes they were an employee and the firm treated them as a contractor; mention that a pending SS-8 still counts.

p. 24, Line 1b, "Enter the total of your wages received as a household employee that was not reported on Form(s) W-2"

findings.who: A filer who itemized on the 2023 return and in 2025 received a refund of 2023 state income tax, for example after an amended state return or a state audit. They had no other recoveries.
findings.why_no: The gate excludes every state or local income tax refund ('other than a state or local income tax refund'), whatever year it is for. The filer truthfully answers no, so the question about a recovery for something deducted before 2024 is never asked.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24, Itemized Deduction Recoveries: 'You can't use the State and Local Income Tax Refund Worksheet ... and must use this discussion if ... 1. You received a refund in 2025 that is for a tax year other than 2024.' p. 27, Worksheet 2: 'complete a separate worksheet for each year.'
findings.fix: Limit the exclusion to the current refund: 'other than a refund of 2024 state or local income tax.' Or have the state refund flow ask which tax year each refund is for, and route a refund for any year before 2024 to rec.before_prior_year.

findings.who: A filer whose recovery came as a credit or offset rather than a payment. Examples: a property tax overpayment credited against the next bill, mortgage interest credited to the loan balance (Form 1098 box 4), a manufacturer rebate or downward price adjustment on an item they took a credit for, or an insurer's reimbursement of a casualty loss deducted in 2023.
findings.why_no: 'Paid back' suggests someone handing back money the filer paid. A bill credit, a price reduction, or an insurance claim payment does not feel like being 'paid back', and the gate's help lists no credit or casualty example.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24: 'The most common recoveries are refunds, reimbursements, and rebates'; p. 28: 'You had a recovery if there was a downward price adjustment or similar adjustment on the item for which you claimed a credit.'
findings.fix: Ask: 'In 2025, did you (or your spouse) receive a refund, reimbursement, rebate, credit on a bill, price reduction, or insurance payment for something you paid in an earlier year?' Add help examples for a casualty loss reimbursement and a rebate on an item you took a credit for. Classify after a yes.

findings.who: A self-employed filer who received a 2025 vendor refund of a 2024 Schedule C expense, a refund of a deducted self-employed health insurance premium, or a refund of student loan interest. They took the standard deduction in 2024.
findings.why_no: The gate's help gives only itemized examples (property tax, sales tax, mortgage interest, medical) and ends with 'Not counted if ... you did not itemize that year.' A standard-deduction filer reads that as 'none of mine count.' A business owner treats vendor refunds as ordinary business receipts, not as a return of something deducted.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 28, Nonitemized Deduction Recoveries: 'If you recover an amount that you deducted in an earlier year when you were figuring your AGI, you must generally include the full amount of the recovery in your income in the year received.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate's help: 'Includes refunds of business expenses, bad debts, or other amounts deducted without itemizing, and rebates on items you took a credit for. These count even if you took the standard deduction.' Also narrow the exclusion sentence so it plainly covers only itemized-only items.

findings.who: A filer who deducted actual general sales tax for 2024 and in 2025 returned a large purchase, such as a car or furniture, getting back the price plus its sales tax.
findings.why_no: They see a store or dealer refund for a returned item, not something 'paid back' that they deducted, and they may not connect the returned purchase to their Schedule A sales tax figure.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24, Example 27: 'In 2025, you return an item you had purchased and receive a $500 sales tax refund ... The maximum refund that you may have to include in income is $500.'
findings.fix: Add to the gate's help: 'Including sales tax refunded when you returned an item bought in an earlier year, if you deducted sales tax that year.'

findings.who: A filer whose 2024 return was prepared by someone else, who in 2025 got an insurance reimbursement of medical bills or a property tax refund. They do not know whether the item was actually deducted, for example because of the 7.5% medical floor or the SALT cap.
findings.why_no: The gate asks them to judge whether the money was 'an amount you deducted or took a credit for', a classification they cannot check. Unsure, they answer no.
findings.irs_text: p525 p. 24, Tax benefit rule: 'You must include a recovery in your income in the year you receive it up to the amount by which the deduction or credit you took for the recovered amount reduced your tax in the earlier year.'
findings.fix: First ask the checkable fact: any refund, reimbursement, or rebate in 2025 of an expense paid in an earlier year. Then ask, or work out from the prior-year return, whether it was deducted or credited and whether the filer itemized.

locators: p. 24, Example 27, "The maximum refund that you may have to include in income is $500 because it’s less than the excess of the tax deducted"
p. 24, Recoveries, "A recovery is a return of an amount you deducted or took a credit for in an earlier year"; p. 26, Example 33, "You must include $50 in your 2025 income, rather than $250"

p. 24, Recoveries, "You may also have recoveries of nonitemized deductions (such as payments on previously deducted bad debts) and recoveries of items for which you previously claimed a tax credit"; p. 25, Caution, "If you also recovered an amount deducted as a nonitemized deduction, figure the amount of that recovery to include in your income and add it to your adjusted gross income (AGI) before applying the rules explained here"

p. 27, Worksheet 2, "If you recovered amounts from more than 1 year, such as a state income tax refund from 2024 and a casualty loss reimbursement from 2023, complete a separate worksheet for each year"; p. 24, Recovery for 2 or more years, "you must allocate, on a pro rata basis, the recovered amount between the years in which you paid it"
p. 27, Worksheet 2, "complete a separate worksheet for each year. Use information from your tax return for the year the expense was deducted"

p. 27, Worksheet 2, footnote 2, "If you deducted state and local general sales taxes and received a refund of those taxes, include the amount on line 2, but don’t enter more than the excess of your sales tax deduction over your state and local income tax you could have deducted"

p. 28, Nonitemized Deduction Recoveries, "This section discusses recovery of deductions other than itemized deductions"; p. 28, Amounts Recovered for Credits, "you must increase your 2024 tax by the amount of the recovery"

findings.who: A church employee of a qualified church-controlled organization that does not fit the help's three named examples—for example, a church-controlled camp, publishing house, or missionary-service organization—whose W-2 boxes 4 and 6 are empty because the organization has an exemption certificate.
findings.why_no: They read 'paid by a church or religious body' as requiring the employer itself to be the church or religious body, and read the help's 'school, hospital or charity' list as the complete set of church-controlled employers that count.
findings.irs_text: i1040sse (2025), p. 1: 'Church employee income is wages you received as an employee … of a church or qualified church-controlled organization that has a certificate in effect electing an exemption from employer social security and Medicare taxes.'
findings.fix: Broaden the gate to include 'or by a qualified church-controlled organization' and make the help examples non-exhaustive, such as 'a school, hospital, charity, camp, publishing house, or mission society controlled by a church or religious body'; then ask the empty-boxes-4-and-6 question for any such employer.

findings.who: An ordained minister whose only 2025 compensation from the church is a rent-free parsonage, utilities, and/or meals and lodging furnished for the church's convenience, with no cash salary or housing allowance.
findings.why_no: The gate asks whether they were 'paid' and the help says 'pay in housing'; the filer treats furnished housing and meals as not being paid and sees no cash amount to report.
findings.irs_text: i1040sse (2025), p. 1: 'Also, include on line 2: • The rental value of a home or an allowance for a home furnished to you (including payments for utilities); and • The value of meals and lodging provided to you, your spouse, and your dependents for your employer’s convenience.'
findings.fix: Ask about compensation in cash or in kind, including parsonage/rental value, utilities, meals, and lodging, rather than only whether the filer was 'paid'; or gate on 'received any compensation or allowance as a minister, religious order member, or Christian Science practitioner.'

locators: , Employees of Churches and Church Organizations, "Church employee income is wages you received as an employee (other than as a minister, member of a religious order, or Christian Science practitioner) of a church or qualified church-controlled organization that has a certificate in effect electing an exemption from employer social security and Medicare taxes"

, Ministers, Members of Religious Orders, and Christian Science Practitioners, "you must pay SE tax on salaries and other income for services you performed as a minister, member of a religious order who hasn’t taken a vow of poverty, or Christian Science practitioner"

findings.who: An S corporation owner-employee leases their personally owned pickup truck or equipment to their own corporation, which pays them a monthly lease amount.
findings.why_no: They see the payment as a business reimbursement or compensation from their own company, not as 'rent'. The help's examples (house, room, vacation home, a car rented on to others) suggest renting to outsiders.
findings.line: scope.rent_personal_if_rental (missed refusal; the personal-property rental is then omitted or put on the wrong schedule)
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 5, Personal property: "Do not use Schedule E to report income and expenses from the rental of personal property, such as equipment or vehicles. Instead, use Schedule C ... If your rental of personal property is not a business, see the instructions for Schedule 1 ... lines 8l and 24b"
findings.fix: Add to help: "Count it even if the renter is your own business or corporation, an employer, or a relative."

findings.who: A filer lets a neighbor use a tractor, trailer or boat for the season and receives hay, labor or other goods or services instead of money.
findings.why_no: Nothing was paid in money, so they don't read 'rent out' or 'receive rent' as covering a swap or barter.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 5, Line 3: "If you received services or property instead of money as rent, report the fair market value of the services or property as rental income"; p527 p. 3: "Rental income is any payment you receive for the use or occupation of property."
findings.fix: Add to help: "Count any payment for the use of your property, including goods, services or a trade instead of money."

findings.who: A filer lists a car on a peer-to-peer car-sharing app, or rents out computer hardware (GPU compute), camera gear or tools through an online marketplace.
findings.why_no: They think of the platform activity as 'sharing', 'hosting' or selling a service rather than renting out something they own.
findings.irs_text: i1040se p. 5, Personal property: "rental of personal property, such as equipment or vehicles"
findings.fix: Add to help: "Including through an app or online platform (car sharing, equipment or computer-hardware marketplaces)."

findings.who: A filer whose lessee of equipment or a vehicle paid them in 2025 to end the lease early, with no other rent received.
findings.why_no: They read the payment as a cancellation fee or settlement, not as rent.
findings.irs_text: p527 p. 3, Canceling a lease: "If your tenant pays you to cancel a lease, the amount you receive is rent."
findings.fix: Add to help: "A payment to cancel or end a lease counts as rent."

locators: Form 1040 (2025), lines 8, 10, 13b, 16, 19–20 and 27–31; , Cash method, "You are a cash basis taxpayer if you report income on your return in the year you actually or constructively receive it, regardless of when it was earned"
p. 5, Personal property, "Do not use Schedule E to report income and expenses from the rental of personal property, such as equipment or vehicles"

p. 24, Line 1h, "The following types of income must be included in the total on line 1h", "Strike or lockout benefits (other than bona fide gifts)"

findings.who: An employee who received only noncash tips in 2025, such as tickets, passes, meals, or other items of value from customers, and no unreported cash or card tips; they may also have ordinary W-2 wages.
findings.why_no: They read the first gate's phrase 'wages, tips, or strike or lockout benefits that are not on a W-2' as asking about cash pay or cash tips, not tickets or other noncash items. Because their W-2 wages are reported and they did not think of noncash items as 'wages' or 'tips' for this question, they answer no; the second helper that expressly mentions 'tips that were not money' is never reached.
findings.irs_text: i1040gi p. 24, Line 1c: 'Also, include the value of any noncash tips you received, such as tickets, passes, or other items of value. Although you don’t report these noncash tips to your employer, you must report them on line 1c.'
findings.fix: Broaden the first gate to ask directly about 'tips of any kind, including noncash tips such as tickets, passes, meals, services, or other items of value,' or remove the parent gate so the noncash-tip question is asked whenever the filer had any tip income.

locators: p. 24, Line 1c, "Also, include the value of any noncash tips you received, such as tickets, passes, or other items of value"

p. 24, Line 1c, "Also, include the value of any noncash tips you received, such as tickets, passes, or other items of value. Although you don’t report these noncash tips to your employer, you must report them on line 1c"
p. 24, Line 1c, "This should include any tip income you didn’t report to your employer", "Also, include the value of any noncash tips you received, such as tickets, passes, or other items of value"

findings.who: A parent or representative files the final 2025 return for a 17-year-old who died in mid-2025 and had $5,000 of interest and dividends. A parent of the child was alive at the end of 2025.
findings.why_no: The helper says 'You were under 24 at the end of 2025'. The child was not alive at the end of 2025, so the person filing may read the question as not applying and answer no.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Who Must File: 'The child either: a. Was under age 18 at the end of 2025 ... 4. At least one of the child's parents was alive at the end of 2025.'
findings.fix: Add help text: 'If you are filing for someone who died during 2025, answer for their age on the date of death.' Or ask for the date of birth (and date of death, if any) and compute the age.

findings.who: A parent uses the tool to prepare their 16-year-old child's own single return. The child has $4,000 of capital gain distributions.
findings.why_no: The parent reads 'You were under 24' as asking about themselves, the person typing, and answers no.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Who Must File: 'Form 8615 must be filed for any child who meets all of the following conditions. 1. The child had more than $2,700 of unearned income.'
findings.fix: Ask 'Was the person this return is for (the taxpayer named on line 1) under 24 at the end of 2025?' Or compute the age from a date of birth the tool already collects.

used.revision: 2025 (the revision for tax year 2025, archived from irs-prior after irs.gov posted a later revision)
locators: p. 1, Who Must File, "The child doesn’t file a joint return for 2025"
p. 1, Who Must File, "The child had more than $2,700 of unearned income"

findings.who: A full-time student aged 19 to 23 whose scholarship or fellowship grant exceeded tuition and required fees, for example $6,000 used for room and board, and was not reported on a Form W-2. A parent is alive and the student has little earned income.
findings.why_no: The question's examples are all investment income ('interest, dividends or gains from investments'). The student does not think of a scholarship as income at all, and certainly not as investment income, so the student answers no.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Unearned Income: "It includes ... taxable scholarship and fellowship grants not reported on Form W-2"
findings.fix: Name every kind of unearned income in the question and help: "...income that was not pay for work, such as interest, dividends, capital gains (including fund distributions), rents, royalties, the taxable part of a scholarship or fellowship grant not on a Form W-2, unemployment compensation, alimony, pension, IRA or annuity distributions (including inherited IRAs), the taxable part of social security, or trust or estate distributions?"

findings.who: A filer under 24 who inherited an IRA or 401(k), for example from a grandparent, and took $8,000 in distributions in 2025, which a Form 1099-R reports. A parent is alive.
findings.why_no: An inherited retirement distribution is neither pay for work nor 'interest, dividends or gains from investments' as the filer understands those words, and the filer sees it as an inheritance.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Unearned Income: "It includes ... pension and annuity income ... and income (other than earned income) received as the beneficiary of a trust"
findings.fix: List retirement distributions (IRA, pension, annuity, including inherited accounts) and trust or estate distributions (Schedule K-1) in the question, or ask about each kind separately and add them up.

findings.who: A minor or student under 24 who received taxable unemployment compensation, or a child receiving survivor or dependent social security benefits with a taxable part, together with other unearned income totaling more than $2,700.
findings.why_no: Unemployment benefits feel like a replacement for wages, and social security benefits feel like a benefit rather than income. Neither matches the investment examples, so the filer leaves them out of the total.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Unearned Income: "It includes ... unemployment compensation, alimony, the taxable part of social security and pension payments"
findings.fix: State explicitly that unemployment compensation and the taxable part of social security count, and tell the filer to add all such amounts together.

findings.who: A child under 18 whose UTMA or UGMA custodial account, held under the child's SSN and managed by a parent, earned $3,500 in dividends and capital gain distributions that were reinvested. Alternatively, a filer under 24 who receives rent or royalty income from property held for them.
findings.why_no: The filer thinks of the custodial account as the parent's money, or reinvested dividends as not 'had'. Rents and royalties are not among the investment examples. Any of these leads the filer to say they had no such income.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Unearned Income: "It includes taxable interest, dividends, capital gains (including capital gain distributions), rents, royalties"
findings.fix: Add to the help: "Count income from accounts held in your name or SSN even if a parent or custodian manages them, including reinvested dividends and fund capital gain distributions, and rents or royalties."

findings.who: A filer with several small kinds of unearned income, for example $1,500 of interest, $900 of dividends and $600 of capital gain distributions, none above $2,700 alone but $3,000 in total.
findings.why_no: The question does not say to add the kinds together. A filer checks each Form 1099 against $2,700 and finds none above it.
findings.irs_text: i8615 p. 1, Who Must File: "The child had more than $2,700 of unearned income"
findings.fix: Ask for the total: "Adding together all of these kinds of income, was the total more than $2,700?" Or collect the amounts and compute the comparison.

used.revision: 2025 (the revision for tax year 2025, archived from irs-prior after irs.gov posted a later revision)
locators: p. 1, Who Must File, "Form 8615 must be filed for any child who meets all of the following conditions"
p. 1, Who Must File, "The child had more than $2,700 of unearned income"
